newsitem.title: ITALY: EU's Monti criticises Italy Eurotax payback plan.
newsitem.headline: EU's Monti criticises Italy Eurotax payback plan.

text.p: EU Commissioner Mario Monti was quoted in an Italian newspaper as saying he was unhappy with a government plan to reimburse taxpayers for a one-off "Euro tax" aimed at smoothing Italy's entry into a currency union.

"The rebate gives the idea more of a loan than of an acquired contribution and this, above all abroad, does not give the perception that it is a measure aimed at reducing the (public) deficit," Monti told Milan daily Corriere della Sera.
The government said on Tuesday it would raise 5.5 trillion lire in 1997 from a one-off income tax surcharge but also committed itself to pay a 60 percent rebate on the sum levied in 1999.

The income tax supplement is part of a 62.5 trillion lire 1997 budget which the government hopes will put Italy firmly on course towards cutting its public deficit to three percent of GDP next year, thereby meeting a key requirement for membership of European economic and monetary union (EMU).

Finance Minister Vicenzo Visco, seen as the architect of the "Eurotax, said the government would stand by its commitment to pay the tax rebate unconditionally if it was still in office in two years time.
"There are no ifs and buts, there are no conditions. This government is committed, if this government remains," Visco told Rome daily La Repubblica in an interview.
Monti also said the government was making a mistake in calling the tax supplement a "Eurotax".

"It could give rise to misunderstandings, make people think that the levy is for the European Union, or that its proceeds are destined for the EU's budget or that it has been imposed at the request of the Commission," said Monti.
"The reduction of the deficit is, instead, in the exclusive interest of Italy," he added. Milan newsroom +392-66102321
